layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Temperature as a Pitting Criterion*

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: R. J. BRIGHAM and E. W. TOZER*

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Abstract

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: On the basis of three independent test methods, two potentiostatically controlled and one freely

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: corroding, temperature has been shown quantitatively to be an important criterion for describing the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: onset of pitting corrosion in molybdenum containing austenitic stainless steels. The temperature at

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: which pitting is initiated in acid chloride solution has been related to the|molybdenum content of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: alloys.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In an earlier presentation,1 the pitting characteristics of a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: series of molybdenum containing austenitic stainless steels

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: were presented as a function of potential and temperature.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: These data, reproduced in Figure 1, are characterized by an

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: intermediate, strongly temperature dependent, potential

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: range which is bracketed at lower and higher potentials by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: plateaus which are insensitive to temperature changes. The

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: upper plateau has been shown to result from the onset of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: transpassivity.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: It is only in the intermediate potential range that the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: relative pitting resistance of the series of alloys can be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: distinguished, and in Figure 1 it is the relative position of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: each of the curves with respect to the temperature axis that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: makes possible a ranking of the alloys. Because the curves

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: for each of the different alloys collectively make up a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: family, the determination of a single point in the inter-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: mediate potential range for each alloy would be indicative

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of the whole curve for that alloy and consequently define

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the relative resistance of each of the alloys.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: A simplified screening test, therefore appears to be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: available in which, at a fixed potential in the intermediate

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: range, the temperature of the solution is increased until

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pitting is observed. This technique would appear to take

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: advantage of the fact that an intermediate potential, such as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: +500 mV (SCE), is common to all of the alloys regardless

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of their relative resistances with respect to temperature and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the steep slope of the temperature-potential curves would

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: suggest a well defined transition.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Increasing Temperature Screening Test

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In this series of experiments, the experimental appara-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tus was the same as that used in the previous investigation.1

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In this case, freshly abraded samples of the experimental

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: alloys listed in Table 1 were exposed in nitrogenated 3.5%

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (0.6M) NaCl pH3 solution and were allowed to corrode

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: freely forfive minutes,usually assuming a potential of -365

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to -370 mV (SCE). The potential was then rapidly increased

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to a value of +500 mV (SCE) and held potentiostatically.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: After a five minutes waiting period, during which the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: current density decreased to the range 1 to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: , the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: FIGURE 1 — Effect of Mo content and temperature on the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: potential required to initiate pitting based on the criterion of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a rise in current density to 10

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in a series of 18% Cr,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: 20% Ni, 0.2%N stainless steels.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: temperature of the solution was increased at the rate of 0.6

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: C per minute. The temperature at which the current density

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: increased sharply to a value of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (the criterion for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pit initiation in Figure 1) was considered to be the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: temperature at which pitting began and was designated

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: For each alloy, multiple runs were carried out.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The results are summarized in Table 2 in terms of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: minimum, maximum, and average

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: values and are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: graphically displayed in Figure 2 with the curves from

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Figure 1. Figure 2 clearly demonstrates the power of this

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: technique in quickly and easily screening a series of alloys

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: for relative resistance to pitting. The excellent correlation

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: confirms the earlier data and takes advantage of the steep

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: slope of the potential-temperature curves in describing

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: relative pitting resistance in terms of a temperature, a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: parameter with possible design significance if the effects of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: testing rate can be taken into account.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Effect of Testing Rate

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The two testing techniques compared above (increasing

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: potential at fixed temperature and increasing temperature

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: at fixed potential) and found to correlate very well are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: based on relatively short term tests. Although it appears

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: that they can be used effectively as a screening test to rank

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the pitting susceptibility of a series of alloys, the signifi-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: cance of these data with respect to long term exposure is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: not immediately clear. Leckie and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: have shown, for

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: increasing potential runs at fixed temperature, that the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: values of critical pitting potential are rate dependent, being

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: more noble at high scan rates for potentials in the general

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: area corresponding to the lower plateau of Figure 1.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: However, Bond and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: found the potential for pitting

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: to be more active at high scan rates, but these results were

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: obtained at generally more noble potentials which would

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: correspond to the potential region near the upper plateau in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Figure 1. On the basis of these observations, extrapolation

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: of the curves of Figure 1 to infinitely slow scan rates would

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: result in an overall increase in slope toward the vertical in

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the intermediate potential range, brought about by further

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: increases in high potential values and decreases in low

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: values. No lateral shift with respect to temperature would

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: be expected in the intermediate potential range, nor are the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: upper plateau pótential values expected to change appre-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ciably in describing infinitely slow scan rates (long exposure

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: times). The lower plateau potential values will, of course,

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: decrease with decreasing scan rate as shown by Leckie and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Uhlig.2

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Shape changes in Figure 1 of the type proposed above

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: would indicate that long term pitting tests should be

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: insensitive to potential over the whole intermediate poten-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: tial range, but very dependent upon test temperature. Data

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: produced at +500 mV (SCE) is apparently near the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: postulated point of rotation of the transition section of the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: curves and should therefore be applicable in predicting long

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: term pitting behavior. To some extent this hypothesis is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: substantiated by the data of Figure 2 which correlate as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: well for the less resistant alloys (short exposure times) as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: for the more resistant alloys (exposure times approaching

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: one hour). Further corroboration was obtained by means of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a series of longer exposures carried out as a function of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: temperature in a solution with oxidizing power in the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: intermediate potential range.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the intermediate potential range defined by Figure 1. After

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Discussion

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The results of the FeCl3 exposure tests (Table 3) agree

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: with the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: values (Table 2) obtained for the same alloys

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: in a solution of similar chloride activity and pH, and the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: values were shown to correlate with the earlier data

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: (Figure 2). It could be argued that this agreement between

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: shorter and longer term tests, one potentiostatically con-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: trolled and the other freely corroding, is fortuitous.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: However, such an agreement is to be expected if the pitting

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: curves in the intermediate potential range of Figure 1

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: approach the vertical for infinitely slow scan rates as

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: postulated above.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Experimental confirmation of the proposed vertical

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: temperature-potential curves in the intermediate potential

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: region to describe infinitely slow scan rates was obtained by

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a series of 66 hour exposure experiments. Samples of 317L

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: stainless steel were exposed to the following solutions of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: similar chloride activities but very different oxidizing

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: power: 16% sodium hypochlorite (domestic bleach) con-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: taining 3.5% NaCl, 10% FeCl3, and 5% potassium ferricya-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: nide containing 3.5% NaCl. In all cases, pitting was

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: observed at a temperature of 30 C or higher, but not at à

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: temperature of 27.5 C or lower. The strong dependence on

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: temperature and not on potential suggests that there exists

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: for each wholly austenitic steel a critical pitting tempera-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ture below which the steel will not pit regardless of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: potential and exposure time. The data presented here are

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: considered to approximate such a parameter.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: In Figure 3, this critical pitting temperature, within the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: limits of accuracy of the techniques described here, is

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: plotted as a function of the Mo content of the various

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: steels, both experimental and commercial. In the case of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: FeCl3 exposure tests, the low temperature end of the error

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: bars plotted in Figure 3 represents the temperature at and

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: below which pitting was not observed, while the high

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: temperature end indicates the temperature at and above

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: temperature by these techniques. The average pitting

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: behavior of all the steels in the composition range 3 to 7.5%

layout_dets.label: ocr_text

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Although the critical pitting temperature of a steel has

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: been obtained in three different but apparently equivalent

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ways, the preferred method appears to be by the use of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: FeCl3 exposures. This technique minimizes testing rate

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: effects, differentiates between pitting and crevice and end

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: grain attack, uses samples of any geometry, and requires a

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: minimum of electronic gadgetry. Regardless of the tech-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: nique used, however, the correlation shown in Figure 3

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: appears to be a valid and workable way of describing the

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pitting susceptibility of wholly austenitic alloys in terms of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: a parameter with design significance.

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: Conclusions

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: The pitting characteristics of molybdenum containing

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: austenitic stainless steel, produced in both experimental 50

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: pound heats and on a commercial scale, have been

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: described by a single parameter, the critical pitting tempera-

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: ture, which depends in a regular way on the Mo content of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: the steel. However, these data are valid only for pit

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: nucleation on a flat surface. Preliminary results indicate that

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: these temperature values should be reduced considerably to

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: describe the onset of edge or crevice attack, which

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: consequently appear to constitute a more likely mode of

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: service failure than pitting. This area is presently under

layout_dets.label: ocr_text
layout_dets.text: investigation.
